# @aponiajs/devtools

> The opt-in devtools surface for a running AponiaJS application. A disabled registration mounts nothing; an enabled one mounts an Elysia plugin that runs at `onStart`, after every route has mounted, and serves an HTTP API bound to loopback by default.

The package is a leaf: nothing in the framework depends on it. An application registers it and decides for itself whether the devtools mount at all — the framework never reads an environment variable on the application's behalf. There are two spellings that mount the same plugin: `DevtoolsModule.register({ enabled })` in a module's `imports`, and `devtoolsPlugin({ enabled })` in `AponiaFactory.create`'s `plugins` option. The option exists because `aponia build` lowers a module only when every `imports` entry names its declaration with a single identifier: a registration is a call expression, so the module path declines the module that wrote it, and a declined root leaves the committed descriptor artifact serving a graph the registration is not in. The option path trades that for a plugin no module declares, so nothing about it reaches the module graph, inspection, or a generated artifact.

## What this package exports

- [DevtoolsModule](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/module/devtools-module.ts): `register(options)` builds the module an application imports; a disabled registration is inert.
- [devtoolsPlugin](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/module/devtools-module.ts): the same plugin for `AponiaFactory.create`'s `plugins` option; a disabled registration answers `undefined`, which mounts nothing.
- [DevtoolsOptions](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/module/devtools-module.types.ts): the required `enabled` switch, the optional `port`, the optional `host` the server binds — loopback unless one is named — the optional `capture` policy `/requests` records under — every option an opt-out, with `redact` empty by default because the tool shows what arrived — and the optional `logger` whose lines `/logs` records, the same object the application gives `AponiaFactory.create`, because the framework never exposes the logger it builds for itself.
- [startDevtoolsServer](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/server/devtools-server.ts): starts the server for one boot on the address it is given, or answers `undefined` when that address is taken.
- [routeRequest](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/server/request-router.ts): the pure dispatcher every request goes through.
- [AponiaMetaPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/meta` payload, including the `contract` version a client checks first.
- [AponiaGraphPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/graph` payload, the compiled module graph with no `routes` key.
- [AponiaRoutesPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/routes` payload, every route the application answers with the binding that serves it.
- [AponiaFlowPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/flow.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/flow` payload, the stages each mounted route passes through and the filters that answer when it throws.
- [createLogBuffer](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/logging/log-buffer.ts): the bounded log stream `/logs` publishes, and the capacity it retains.
- [tapLogBuffer](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/logging/log-tap.ts): records everything a `LoggerService` writes into a buffer, patching the logger in place and answering the stream that records it — one logger, one stream — or `undefined` when nothing could be installed on the logger, which is why a logger it cannot patch is never published as one. The stream it answers with states the levels the tap reached beside the buffer that records them, because an entry names only the level it was written at: without that list a level nothing was written at and a level the tap never installed into would read the same.
- [AponiaLogsPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/logs` payload, the entries after one cursor, the cursor to poll from next, and the levels the stream reached.
- [AponiaRequestsPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/requests` payload, the requests that reached the record after one cursor — one entry when a request arrives and one when it is answered, both carrying the request's `id` — and the cursor to poll from next.
- [AponiaAotPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/aot.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/aot` payload — the graph the container compiled and the boot's verdict on the generated invoker artifact, beside a build's per-handler verdicts for the project the server was started in.
- [createRequestBuffer](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/requests/request-buffer.ts): the bounded request record `/requests` publishes, and the capacity a registration retains.

## Behavior a consumer can rely on

- A disabled module registers no provider, mounts no plugin, and opens no socket.
- An enabled module registers an `ElysiaPluginModule`, so its plugin runs at `onStart` — after every route has mounted.
- `onStart` fires on `listen()`. An application that only calls `handle()` publishes nothing and is unaffected.
- The bind address is `127.0.0.1` unless the registration names a `host`. A loopback address — `127.0.0.1`, any `127.x.x.x`, `::1`, `localhost` — binds silently; anything else is permitted and reported once under `Devtools`, naming the `host` option, the address the socket took, and `/requests`, which records request headers and bodies by default.
- A port that is already bound is reported under `Devtools` and never fails the boot: the application answers its own routes without the devtools server.
- The devtools socket stops when the application is closed, so a restart binds a fresh one.
- `GET /__devtools/meta` reports the contract version — `2` in this release — the release that booted the application, the Elysia installed in the application's own tree (`null` when there is none), and which release supplied each artifact the boot adopted (`null` for one it did not).
- `GET /__devtools/graph` reports the graph the application compiled: its modules with their imports, controllers, providers, dependencies and exports, and its WebSocket gateways with their events. It describes the descriptor artifact's graph when the boot adopted one and the lowered decorated classes otherwise, and it carries no routes.
- `GET /__devtools/routes` reports the routes the application answers, read from the mounted table when the request arrives, so a route mounted after the boot appears too. Each route carries the method and path the table states, the module, controller and handler the boot recorded, the context fields its handler binds, and `source`: `"generated"` for a build-time invoker, `"compiled"` for the running platform's own binding, or `null` when no boot recorded the route. A route no record describes reports empty names rather than guessed ones.
- `GET /__devtools/flow` reports the stages each mounted route passes through and the filters that answer when it throws, read from the mounted table when the request arrives. The stages a route's hooks and schema state come from that table; the stages its guards and interceptors state come from the compiled plan, because the platform lowered them into one `beforeHandle` and one `afterHandle` where their order is no longer legible, so each names the class it runs. A compiled hook is published as its parts and never as a hook stage, and a contributed hook is identified by the checksum Elysia stamps rather than by a plugin name the route does not carry. Filters are a list beside the stages, never a stage in the chain. Which interceptor halves a route runs is the boot's own record, read from the instance the platform calls while the class resolved, so a half declared as a class field (`interceptBefore = () => {}`) is published like any other; a record that carries no such field — a copy of the platform older than this release — falls back to each class token's `prototype`, which answers for the class the token names rather than for the object the platform calls, so it is wrong in both directions: it publishes a half only when that token declares one there, which omits a field-declared half, and it states one for a token whose provider supplied an object of another shape — the object the platform calls in its place.
- `GET /__devtools/logs?since=<cursor>` reports what the application logged: the registration patches the logger the application passes as `logger` — the same object it gives `AponiaFactory.create` — and records every line into a bounded buffer from the moment the module registers, so the lines a boot writes about itself are included. An answer carries `{ cursor, entries, levels }` with each entry shaped `{ level, context, message, timestamp }`; `levels` names the `LoggerService` levels the tap reached on the logger it was handed, so a level the logger does not declare, or one whose assignment refused the patch, is stated as unreached rather than left to be inferred from an absent entry. A cursor older than the retained window answers what is retained and one ahead of every write answers nothing, so a poll is never an error, and the cursor never goes backwards. A registration with nothing to record from — an omitted option, `logger: false`, a level array the platform builds a logger from, or a logger object whose first level refuses the patch — serves no `/logs` rather than an empty stream, because an empty stream would announce that nothing is being logged while an application that handed the factory a logger logs normally. A logger that accepts one level's patch and refuses the next one's is not that case: a level was patched before the refusal, so the stream is served, the refusing level keeps the method it had, and every level after it is still patched. The levels reached are published rather than left to be inferred: `levels` names them, so a stream that never carries `debug` is told apart from one whose tap never reached `debug`. The one filter the stream cannot read is the logger's own — `LoggerService` has no notion of an enabled level, so a line the console would have suppressed is still recorded.
- `GET /__devtools/requests?since=<cursor>` reports the requests that reached the record and what answered them. One request writes two entries and both carry the same `id`, so a consumer groups by `id` and takes the last entry for each request; the first is written when the request arrives and states `status: null` and `durationMs: null`, which is this record saying it saw the request and saw nothing answer it — a plugin that answered from its own `onRequest` before any later phase ran, for instance — rather than an invented status or a missing entry, and it states the path that arrived because no route has matched yet. Both hook phases run in mount order, so a plugin mounted ahead of the devtools registration that answers from its own `onRequest` ends the request before this record's hook runs, and that request appears nowhere. Everything is recorded by default and every option under `capture` is an opt-out, never a permission: an entry carries the `method`, the `path` — the route pattern that matched, or the path that arrived when none did — the `url` as it arrived, the `status`, the `durationMs`, the `timestamp`, the request's `headers`, and the `body` the route parsed, truncated at `capture.bodyLimit`, while a body this package cannot serialize is stored as `[unserializable]` rather than left out, because a missing `body` would read as a request that carried none, and a body that arrived as a literal JSON `null` is stored as the text `null` for the same reason. `error` carries the failure's message: what the answer published, or — for an unhandled failure the platform mapped — the exception that mapping answered. It is present on a `5xx` whose Problem Details body the tool can read and on the mapped failure named below, absent on a `4xx`, which is an answer rather than a failure, and absent where there is nothing to read — a `5xx` a handler built itself. The mapped failure is the one whose message comes from the exception rather than the answer: the mapping answers one fixed sentence for every such failure and its `Response` is not on the after-response context either, so the boot records the exception the mapping answered, and the entry publishes the same one-line account `/logs` states for it, with no stack — and a value that refuses both the JSON form and the plain string form is stated as the literal `[unprojectable]`, because a throw on that line would take the answer with it. A token passed as a query parameter is captured in `url`, which is a fact about the record rather than a defect in it: `capture.redact`, empty by default, replaces named headers with `[redacted]`. `durationMs` is measured from the moment the request reached this package's arrival hook to a reading the completion path takes before its first read of the context, so the route, the status, the parsed body — and the one microtask spent reading a readable `5xx` answer's published body — are outside it; the arrival hook's own URL and header capture remains inside, and the field is not "the time the application spent on the route". A request that matched no route has no route identity — `path` carries the path that arrived, and `/routes` is the table that tells the two apart. The record belongs to one application and one boot: two applications in one process, and two registrations, keep their own windows, and a second `listen()` begins a new empty one rather than extending the window a socket that is gone was serving. A registration told to capture nothing still serves `/requests`, answering an empty record rather than no endpoint, and writes no arrival entry either. An answer carries `{ cursor, entries }` under the same cursor rules as `/logs`, except that its cursor counts entries rather than requests — one request writes two of them — so a poll is never an error and the cursor never goes backwards.
- `GET /__devtools/aot` reports what a build decided beside what the boot did with it. `graph` — the root the container compiled — and `invokers` — the boot's verdict on the generated invoker artifact, with the refusal's own sentence and no `reason` key at all when there was no refusal — come from the boot record, so they are answered whether or not a project is on disk. `controllers` comes from `@aponiajs/cli`'s analysis of the project the process was started in — the source root `aponia.json` names, walked the way `aponia build` walks it — and gives each handler's verdict: `"generated"` when the emitter renders an invoker for it, `"compiled"` when it declines and the running platform keeps compiling it, with the emitter's own reason. A handler is one property key, however many route decorators it carries. The analyzer is imported on the first request to this endpoint and never at boot, and its result is cached for the life of the process, so an application that never polls this endpoint never loads `ts-morph`. A project the analysis cannot read — no `aponia.json`, no controller under the source root, a source root outside the project, two controllers sharing one class name, an analyzer that would not load — leaves `controllers` empty and reports the reason once under `Devtools`, while the boot's own facts are still answered. A project whose every handler was declined still reports those verdicts, because they are what the endpoint exists to explain. The endpoint is served only for a record that states the two boot facts it publishes; a record that does not is answered with `404` while every other endpoint this server serves keeps answering. That is a different failure from a project the analysis cannot read, which still answers with the boot's half and an empty `controllers`.
- Every endpoint is a `GET`. Any other method answers `405` before the path is read, and a path the server does not serve answers `404`.
